newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan army to halt action against UNITA - Beye.
newsitem.headline: Angolan army to halt action against UNITA - Beye.

text.p: The government has agreed to halt a month-long military campaign to break the opposition UNITA movement's hold on Angola's rich diamond fields, U.N. special representative Alioune Blondin Beye said at the weekend.
Beye, who acknowledged officially on Friday that fighting had erupted between the government and Jonas Savimbi's UNITA, told Reuters late on Saturday the army would seek no further gains.

"We have asked that the government stop this military operation and they have agreed," said Beye, head of the U.N. Angola Verification Mission (UNAVEM) and chairman of a Joint Commission overseeing implementation of a 1994 peace accord.
Beye said the United Nations had not asked the government to withdraw from the 10 border districts taken from UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, since mid-May.
"We do not feel we should work like that at this moment. We have received assurances from the government that the operation will stop. At this point we think that is enough," he said.

Beye, scheduled to fly to New York on Monday to brief the U.N. Security Council on the peace process in Angola, said he expected Savimbi and President Jose Eduardo dos Santos to meet soon to discuss the future of the country's diamond fields.
"The diamond issue is delicate. It is a politically sensitive issue, but its settlement would certainly help to facilitate permanent peace in Angola.

"We are encouraging it, but it is up to the two leaders to come together. As far as I know, when the next meeting takes place between them, it will be in Angola. I am not aware of any change of venue," Beye said.
Industry analysts estimate Angola produces diamonds worth up to $1 billion a year, mostly from regions under UNITA's control.
The border regions taken by the government over the past month probably accounted for around 10 percent of the production from UNITA-held areas, they said.
Diplomats and officials close to the peace process here have long said the key to increasing diamond output lies in direct negotiations between Savimbi and Dos Santos.
Diamonds and the country's offshore oilfields hold the best prospect of rebuilding the country, which was devastated by civil war and is now among the world's poorest.

Beye said the United Nations would not curtail the mandate of the UNAVEM force, which is supervising a programme to disarm and demobilise most of the forces who battled for almost 20 years after independence from Portugal in 1975.

About 60 UNITA members have taken up seats in the National Assembly since April, but Savimbi has not accepted any role in government and diplomats say he still controls up to 70 percent of the country.

The government has insisted its operations in the Lunda Norte Province since May 18 have been to seal the border against armed rebels from Rwanda and the former Zaire. UNITA insists the goal has been control of the diamond fields.

The army action has been the biggest in over two years. Though UNAVEM reports only skirmishes and localised conflict, military and diplomatic sources say there have been fierce clashes with many casualties.
UNITA has complained that compliance with terms of the 1994 Lusaka accord that ended the 20-year civil war has left it defenceless against the government troops.
Military analysts and diplomats in Luanda say, though, that UNITA maintains up to 10,000 heavily armed soldiers. The Angolan government says the former rebels have a standing army of some 35,000.

Beye is scheduled to discuss the future of the U.N.'s mission in Angola during his New York visit. He said the withdrawal of over 5,000 peace-keepers would depend on the political situation in the country.
